Phase 1 -- system map: document the analyzed service's components, external
dependencies, and entry points as SystemComponent entries (kind: service, worker, job,
external-dependency, datastore, or entrypoint), each with a stable ID and a
description; record dependencies between components via `depends_on`. Propose every
entry through the `propose_edits` tool, tagged for phase 1 -- free-form text never
changes the artifacts.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.
I'll start by loading the tool schemas and exploring the codebase.

payload_or_id.description: kvstore.api.get_value(cache, key) -- the only client-facing operation the service exposes. Delegates to Cache.get, converts a StorageError into an 'error'-labeled increment of kvstore_get_value_requests_total and re-raises; otherwise increments the 'success' label and returns the value. This is the sole point in the package where any metric is emitted, and it cannot distinguish a correct value from a stale or wrong one served out of cache.

kvstore.cache.Cache -- unbounded in-memory dict of key -> Entry(value, inserted_at_ms) sitting in front of Storage. On a hit it returns the cached value without ever re-consulting storage; on a miss it reads through to Storage and caches the result (including a None 'key absent' result). It expires nothing itself: bounding the cache is entirely delegated to the background evictor, and invalidating an entry after a write is entirely delegated to whoever writes. It exposes items() for the evictor to walk and evict(key) for eviction/invalidation. Uninstrumented: no hit/miss, size, or entry-age signal leaves this component.

kvstore.storage.Storage -- the backing key-value store, implemented as a single delimited flat file holding one 'key,value' pair per line. get() linearly scans the whole file per lookup and returns None when the file is absent or the key is not found; put() reads the entire file, merges the new pair into a dict, and rewrites the file whole (non-atomic, no locking). Both wrap OSError in StorageError. Line format is unescaped, so keys/values containing the delimiter or a newline are not round-tripped faithfully. Uninstrumented: no latency, size, or error-type signal of its own.

The local filesystem path backing Storage (the flat file plus its parent directory, created on demand by put()). External to the service's process: its availability, permissions, free space, and durability are owned by the host, and any failure there surfaces to the service only as an OSError wrapped in StorageError. It is also shared mutable state between the read path and the write path with no locking or atomic replace.

kvstore.evictor.run_eviction_pass(cache) -- background pass, intended to be driven repeatedly by a scheduler loop, that walks Cache.items() and evicts every entry older than TTL_SECONDS (300s), returning the number removed so a caller can observe progress. It is the only mechanism bounding cache memory and the only mechanism that ever ages a stale cache entry out. It compares a seconds-based `now` against a milliseconds-based Entry.inserted_at_ms, so the expiry condition is never true and the pass always evicts zero entries. Its return value is currently observed by nothing.

The scheduler/loop external to this package that is expected to invoke run_eviction_pass on an interval. It is not implemented anywhere in the repository, so both its existence and its period are assumptions: if it is never wired up, misconfigured, or dies, eviction silently stops with no signal from inside the service.

kvstore.admin.update_value(storage, cache, key, value) -- internal, non-client-facing write path, described as being driven by a periodic data-sync job. It calls Storage.put only. It receives the Cache but never calls cache.evict(key), so a key already present in the cache keeps serving the pre-write value indefinitely. Uninstrumented: no write count, success/failure, or freshness signal is emitted.

The periodic data-sync caller external to this package that drives admin.update_value. Not implemented in the repository, so its schedule, batch semantics, and error handling are assumptions. It is the origin of every write into the system, so its stalling or failing is indistinguishable, from inside the service, from there being no new data to write.

prometheus_client's default registry and whatever exposition endpoint and scraper collect from it. It carries the service's only metric today, kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}. No exposition endpoint is started anywhere in the repository, so whether these counters ever reach a scrapeable sink is an unverified assumption; if they do not, every metric-based alert built on this service is silently dead.

event.text:
Phase 1 complete — 9 `SystemComponent` entries accepted into `system-map.yaml`.

**The service:** `kvstore`, a read-through cache over a flat-file store. One client-facing operation, `get_value`.

| ID | Kind | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `sm-api-get-value` | entrypoint | `api.get_value` — sole public surface, sole metric emitter |
| `sm-cache-layer` | service | unbounded in-memory dict, never self-expires |
| `sm-storage-layer` | datastore | `Storage` — full-file scan on read, full-file rewrite on write |
| `sm-storage-file` | external-dependency | the backing file + filesystem |
| `sm-evictor-worker` | worker | `run_eviction_pass` — sole bound on cache size |
| `sm-eviction-scheduler` | external-dependency | assumed caller of the evictor (not in repo) |
| `sm-admin-write-path` | job | `admin.update_value` — internal write path |
| `sm-data-sync-job` | external-dependency | assumed driver of writes (not in repo) |
| `sm-metrics-registry` | external-dependency | prometheus registry + scrape path |

**Dependency shape:** `api → cache → storage → file`, with `evictor → cache` and `admin → storage` (and, notably, `admin → cache` as a dependency it holds but never uses).

Three things stood out while mapping, which I've recorded in the descriptions because they set up the failure chains for phase 2:

1. **The only instrumented point is the outermost one.** Everything below `api.get_value` — cache hit/miss, cache size, storage latency, eviction counts, write volume — is silent. A chain that starts three hops in has exactly one place it can surface, and only if it changes the success/error ratio there.
2. **Two components in the map exist only as assumptions.** Neither the eviction scheduler nor the data-sync job is implemented in the repo. I mapped them as external dependencies rather than omitting them, because "the thing that was supposed to call this never ran" is a failure mode that needs an owner in the map to hang off.
3. **`admin_write_path` depends on `cache_layer` but never invalidates it.** I recorded the dependency edge as it exists in the signature rather than as it's exercised, since the gap between the two is itself the defect.

I also flagged, on `sm-metrics-registry`, that no exposition endpoint is started anywhere in the repo. If that holds, every alert phases 3 and 4 produce would be dead on arrival — I'll treat confirming the scrape path as a prerequisite rather than assuming it.

Ready for phase 2 (failure modes) when you are.

Phase 2 -- failure modes: document every way this service can fail as FailureMode
entries, each with a stable ID, a severity (`critical` demands immediate human
intervention and pages; `warning` demands action soon and files a ticket), a
`user_visible` flag, and -- for a user-visible failure -- its upstream causes named by
`caused_by`, each of which must itself be a documented entry with its own severity and
visibility. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for phase 2.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

payload_or_id.name: Reader served a stale value indefinitely after a write
payload_or_id.description: A key is written through admin.update_value, but any client whose key was already cached keeps receiving the pre-write value. There is no upper bound on how long this lasts: the only mechanism that would ever age the entry out is the evictor, which never expires anything. get_value returns outcome='success' throughout, so the service reports perfect health while serving data that is arbitrarily old.

payload_or_id.name: Key written after a negative cache fill is never visible
payload_or_id.description: A read for a key that does not yet exist caches Entry(value=None) permanently. When the data-sync job later writes that key, the cache keeps answering None. The client sees 'key does not exist' forever for a key that demonstrably does exist in storage. Distinct from stale-read because the poisoning read need not follow a write -- merely asking for a key too early is enough to make it permanently invisible.

payload_or_id.name: Process memory exhaustion from unbounded cache growth
payload_or_id.description: Every distinct key ever read adds a permanent dict entry. Under sustained unique-key traffic the cache grows without bound until the process is OOM-killed or degrades into GC thrash, taking the whole read path down. This is a total outage arriving with no prior warning on the one metric that exists: the request counter looks healthy right up to the moment the process dies.

payload_or_id.name: get_value raises StorageError to the client
payload_or_id.description: A cache miss reaches Storage.get, the underlying read fails with OSError, and the wrapped StorageError propagates out of get_value to the caller. The client gets an exception rather than a value. This is the one user-visible failure the existing instrumentation already reflects, as a rise in kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome='error'}.

payload_or_id.name: Every key reported absent after the backing file disappears
payload_or_id.description: If the backing file is deleted, or its volume is unmounted or mounted empty, Storage.get takes the `not self._path.exists()` branch and returns None rather than raising. Every read then answers 'key not found' and is counted as outcome='success'. The cache compounds it: each such read is stored as a permanent negative entry, so the fault survives the file being restored. A complete data outage that is, to every existing signal, indistinguishable from clients simply asking for keys that were never written.

payload_or_id.name: Client served a value belonging to a different key, or a truncated one
payload_or_id.description: The flat-file format is unescaped and line-oriented, so a value containing a comma is truncated at the first comma on read-back, and a key or value containing a newline injects a second line that is parsed as an unrelated key-value pair -- letting one write silently overwrite or fabricate another key. A read racing a whole-file rewrite can also observe a truncated file. In all cases get_value returns a plausible-looking wrong string, counted as a success. Silent data corruption is the worst class of failure here because downstream consumers act on it.

payload_or_id.name: Keys permanently lost from the backing store
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put rewrites the entire file in place with no temp-file-and-rename and no lock. A crash, a disk-full condition, or a second concurrent writer during that rewrite leaves the store truncated or missing whichever updates lost the race. The affected keys are gone from the only durable copy; subsequent reads return None as a success. Unrecoverable without an external backup.

payload_or_id.name: Read latency grows with the size of the backing file
payload_or_id.description: Every cache miss reads and linearly scans the whole file, and every write rewrites it whole. As the key set grows, miss latency and write cost grow linearly with total stored data rather than with the data actually requested. Clients see steadily worsening response times with no step change to point at. Degradation rather than outage, so it warrants a ticket rather than a page -- but it is unbounded and ends in one.

payload_or_id.name: Whole dataset goes stale because writes stopped arriving
payload_or_id.description: If the periodic data-sync job stops running, or its writes start failing, no new data enters the store at all. Reads keep succeeding against increasingly old data. From inside the service this is indistinguishable from a period with genuinely no new data, because nothing counts writes -- the absence of a signal is the only symptom, and absence is exactly what the current instrumentation cannot report.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction pass never expires anything (seconds vs milliseconds)
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass computes `now = time.time()` in seconds and compares it against Entry.inserted_at_ms, recorded in milliseconds. `now - entry.inserted_at_ms` is therefore always a large negative number and never exceeds TTL_SECONDS, so the expired-key list is always empty and the pass evicts nothing on every run. The bug is live today and is the shared root of both unbounded cache growth and permanently stale entries. The pass still returns 0 and appears to complete normally, which is why it reads as working.

payload_or_id.name: Nothing invokes the eviction pass
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass has no caller in the repository. Whatever scheduler is meant to drive it lives outside this package, so it may never have been wired up, may be misconfigured to too long an interval, or may have died. Independent of the unit-mismatch bug: fixing that one still leaves eviction dead if nothing calls the function. Both must hold for the cache to stay bounded, and neither is currently observable.

payload_or_id.name: Eviction pass outcome is discarded by its caller
payload_or_id.description: run_eviction_pass returns the number of entries removed specifically so a caller can observe progress, and nothing in the repository consumes that return value or records the pass having run. This is what makes the two failures above silent rather than merely present: a pass that evicts zero every time, and a pass that never runs at all, produce identical evidence, namely none.

payload_or_id.name: Write path never invalidates the cached entry
payload_or_id.description: admin.update_value takes a Cache parameter and calls only storage.put, never cache.evict(key). Cache.evict exists and is correct; it is simply not called from the writer. Because Cache.get never re-consults storage for an already-cached key, this makes every write invisible to any reader that has touched that key -- and with eviction broken there is no fallback path that eventually reconciles the two.

payload_or_id.name: Key-absent results are cached permanently
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get stores the result of a miss unconditionally, including a None meaning 'no such key'. A negative result is thus cached with the same permanence as a real value. This converts two otherwise-transient conditions -- reading a key before it is written, and reading while the backing file is missing -- into permanent per-key failures, which is why it appears as an upstream cause of two separate user-visible modes.

payload_or_id.name: Cache has no capacity bound or admission policy
payload_or_id.description: The cache is a plain dict with no maximum entry count, no memory ceiling, and no LRU or other replacement policy. Size is bounded solely by TTL eviction succeeding. That makes correct eviction load-bearing for process survival rather than merely an optimisation, and it means a burst of unique keys within one TTL window can exhaust memory even if eviction is working perfectly.

payload_or_id.name: Every read scans the entire backing file
payload_or_id.description: Storage.get calls read_text() on the whole file and scans it line by line for a match, so a single-key lookup costs O(total stored data) in both I/O and memory. There is no index, no seek, and no streaming -- the entire file is materialised in memory per lookup, which is also a memory spike proportional to store size on every cache miss.

payload_or_id.name: Backing file grows monotonically with the key set
payload_or_id.description: The store has no deletion operation and no compaction, so the file only ever grows as the data-sync job introduces new keys. Combined with the linear scan above, this makes read cost a function of everything ever written rather than of what is being read, and steadily raises the cost of every write, since each put rewrites the whole file.

payload_or_id.name: Writes truncate and rewrite the file in place
payload_or_id.description: Storage.put reads the whole file, merges one pair, and calls write_text on the same path -- truncating the only durable copy before the replacement content is written, with no temp file, no atomic rename, and no fsync. Any interruption between truncation and completion leaves a partial or empty store. The window scales with file size, so this failure becomes more likely as the store grows.

payload_or_id.name: Concurrent writers silently lose updates
payload_or_id.description: put is an unlocked read-modify-write over the whole file. Two writers overlapping means the second to finish rewrites the file from a snapshot taken before the first one's change, discarding it. No error is raised to either writer -- both believe they succeeded. Whether this is reachable depends on whether the data-sync job is ever concurrent with itself or with another writer, which the repository does not settle.

payload_or_id.name: Reads observe a partially written file
payload_or_id.description: Because writes are not atomic, a reader calling read_text while a rewrite is in flight can observe a truncated file or a partial final line. The reader raises no error: it either fails to find a key that exists, or parses a partial line into a wrong key-value pair. Unlike the delimiter defect, this is transient and load-dependent, which makes it far harder to reproduce from the resulting user report.

payload_or_id.name: Keys and values are not escaped for the file format
payload_or_id.description: Pairs are joined with a comma and split with partition(','), with no escaping or quoting on either side. A value containing a comma is silently truncated at the first one on read-back. A key or value containing a newline writes an extra physical line that is later parsed as a separate pair, letting one write create or clobber an unrelated key. Data-dependent rather than load-dependent: it fires the first time the data-sync job carries a value with a comma in it.

payload_or_id.name: Backing file exists but cannot be read
payload_or_id.description: The file is present but read_text raises OSError -- permissions changed, the underlying device errors, an NFS mount hangs or returns EIO, or the file descriptor limit is hit. payload_or_id.name: Backing file cannot be written

| ID | Sev | Coverage |
|---|---|---|
| `fm-stale-read-after-write` | critical | metric-gap |

| `fm-durable-data-loss` | critical | metric-gap |

Phase 3 complete.

**Implemented metrics: one.** `kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome}` (`api.py:19-23`), a counter with two label values, emitted at two call sites. That is the entire instrumentation surface of the codebase — confirmed by grep across all sources. No exposition endpoint exists anywhere in the repo.

**Coverage across the 29 failure modes:**

| Status | Count |
|---|---|
| `alertable` | 2 |
| `metric-gap` | 24 |
| `excluded` | 3 |

The two alertable modes are `fm-read-unavailable` and its cause `fm-storage-file-unreadable` — the same `outcome="error"` series covers both, which is correct here since there's no remediation difference between them at that layer.

**16 metric recommendations** — 14 new, 2 changes to the existing counter.

Highest-value first:

1. **`mr-storage-read-results`** — splits storage reads into `found` / `not_found` / `file_absent` / `error`. Closes the worst gap in the service: a deleted file or unmounted volume currently reports a 100% success rate. `file_absent` should be zero always, so the alert needs no baseline.
2. **`mr-cache-oldest-entry-age` + `mr-eviction-entries-removed`** — together conclusive on the live evictor bug. Zero removals alone is legitimate; zero removals *while an entry is older than TTL* is not. I specified that the age gauge must be computed from raw `inserted_at`, **not** by reusing the evictor's comparison — otherwise the metric inherits the bug it exists to detect.
3. **`mr-write-leaves-stale-cache`** — fires at the moment staleness is created rather than when a client complains, and is self-retiring: once `cache.evict()` is added it stays flat by construction, so it doubles as the regression test.
4. **`mr-storage-size`** — the store has no delete operation, so key count is monotonically non-decreasing by construction. Any drop is unambiguous data loss. No threshold to tune.

The two changes to the existing counter: add a `not_found` outcome, and catch `BaseException` rather than only `StorageError`. The second matters more than it looks — unanticipated failures currently increment neither label, so they vanish from the denominator of any error ratio, including the `MemoryError` that would precede the OOM.

**Three reasoned exclusions,** all for the same reason: they're standing properties or absences of instrumentation, true at every instant, so an alert on them either always fires or never does. `fm-eviction-progress-unobserved`, `fm-cache-unbounded-no-capacity-limit`, `fm-storage-linear-scan`. Each is remediated by a metric and alerted via its *consequence* instead — I recorded which one in every case, so none of them dead-ends.

**Two things I want to flag rather than bury:**

- I raised an **amendment to phase 2** and applied it. Those three exclusions were recorded as `metric-gap` in `failure-modes.yaml` during phase 2; leaving them would have had the two artifacts asserting different things about the same modes. Now reconciled, with `exclusion_reason` on each.

Phase 4 -- alert recommendations: for every non-excluded failure mode, recommend at

serving several failure modes carries the highest severity among them. No failure mode

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the

Write every alert expression as PromQL — this stack's expression language.

Each recommended alert is an `AlertRuleInput` with every one of these fields

- `name`: the alert's identifier.
- `expr`: the PromQL expression that fires the alert, at most

- `for_duration`: how long the expression must hold before firing, as a Prometheus

- `annotations`: a dict whose required keys are `summary` (a short one-line

annotations.summary: More than 1% of get_value calls are failing with StorageError
annotations.description: get_value is raising StorageError to clients, meaning cache misses are reaching the backing file and the read is failing -- permissions, a device error, a hung mount, or fd exhaustion. This is the only failure mode the pre-existing instrumentation could already detect, and the only one in kvstore that surfaces as an exception rather than as a wrong or absent value. The clamp_min guard keeps the ratio defined when traffic is zero, which would otherwise produce a 0/0 NaN and silently never fire. Serves the user-visible failure and its upstream cause with one rule deliberately: at this layer there is no remediation difference between them.

annotations.summary: get_value is failing with exceptions other than StorageError
annotations.description: Requests are failing in ways the original instrumentation could not see at all. Before the mr-api-catch-all-errors change, any exception other than StorageError incremented neither label, so such requests vanished from the total entirely and the error ratio was computed over a denominator that had silently dropped exactly the unanticipated failures an error-rate alert exists to catch. Any non-zero rate here is a bug worth a ticket. Note this rule cannot fire until that change lands -- it is recommended together with the instrumentation, not against today's code. A MemoryError appearing here is the last warning before the OOM chain completes and should be escalated immediately rather than triaged as a warning.

annotations.summary: The backing store file is missing -- reads are answering 'not found' for every key
annotations.description: Storage.get is taking its file-does-not-exist branch, which returns None rather than raising. Every read is therefore answering 'key not found' and, without the mr-storage-read-results split, would be counted as outcome='success' -- a complete data outage reported as perfect health. Likely causes are a deleted file, an unmounted or empty-mounted volume, or a wrong path in configuration. The cache compounds it: each such read is stored as a permanent negative entry, so the fault survives the file being restored and may require a process restart to clear. This series should be zero at all times, so the threshold needs no baseline and no tuning; the 2m for_duration exists only to ride out a scrape landing mid-deploy.

annotations.summary: Over half of get_value calls are returning no value
annotations.description: The client-visible end of the data-outage chain: the service is answering 'no such key' for the majority of requests. Complements KvstoreStorageFileAbsent rather than duplicating it -- the storage-layer signal fades as the cache fills with permanent negative entries, and this one takes over at exactly that point, because it is measured where clients actually experience the failure. It also catches the poisoned-key case, where a read that arrived before the data-sync job wrote the key leaves a negative entry that never expires. The 0.5 threshold is the one number here that depends on the workload: a service whose clients legitimately probe for absent keys needs it raised, and the correct value should be read off the not_found ratio during known-good operation before this rule is enabled.

annotations.summary: A large share of reads are served 'no such key' from cache without consulting storage
annotations.description: Cache.get is returning cached None values, meaning the service is confidently answering 'no such key' from memory for keys it has not re-checked against storage since the first miss. Because negative entries are cached with the same permanence as real values and eviction is the only thing that would ever clear them, a rising ratio means an accumulating population of keys that can never become visible even after they are written. Scoped to this single failure mode on purpose, and kept at warning: the user-visible consequences are alerted separately by KvstoreNotFoundRatioHigh at critical, and promoting this rule to match would page on a ratio that is legitimately high for workloads that probe for absent keys. The 30m for_duration reflects that this is an accumulating condition, not a step change.

annotations.summary: Cache entries are surviving well past their TTL -- expiry is not working
annotations.description: An entry is alive at more than twice TTL_SECONDS (300s), which proves expiry is not happening. Deliberately indifferent to why: it fires for the known seconds-versus-milliseconds bug in run_eviction_pass, for a scheduler that never invokes the pass, and for any future regression in either, so it keeps working after the current bug is fixed. This is also the closest available bound on staleness exposure -- entry age bounds how old a served value can be -- which is why it serves the stale-read and invisible-key chains as well. The 600s threshold is 2x TTL and must be raised together with TTL_SECONDS if that constant ever changes; the two are coupled and will drift apart silently otherwise.

annotations.summary: The eviction pass is running but removing nothing while entries are past TTL
annotations.description: The sharper diagnosis of the same fault KvstoreCacheEntriesNeverExpire detects, kept separate because it points an operator at the code rather than at the scheduler. Neither half is conclusive alone: zero removals is entirely legitimate when nothing has aged out yet, and an old entry could be explained by a pass that has not run recently. Together they are conclusive -- something should have been removed and was not. This is the exact signature of the live bug, where run_eviction_pass compares a seconds-based now against a milliseconds-based inserted_at, making the expired condition permanently false and the return value permanently 0.

annotations.summary: Nothing has invoked the eviction pass recently
annotations.description: Answers the separate question 'did the pass run at all', which is what tells an operator to look at the scheduler rather than at the eviction code. run_eviction_pass has no caller anywhere in the kvstore repository, so the scheduler is external and may never have been wired up, may be misconfigured to too long an interval, or may have died. This is independent of the arithmetic bug: fixing that leaves eviction just as dead if nothing calls the function, and eviction is the only thing bounding cache memory. The absent() arm matters as much as the increase() arm, because a pass that has never run once produces no series to compare against.

annotations.summary: Cache is on track to exhaust memory within hours
annotations.description: The leading indicator for the OOM chain, and the only rule in this set that gives time to act before a total outage: the pre-existing request counter looks perfectly healthy right up to the moment the process is killed, then simply stops. Uses predict_linear rather than a static ceiling because the failure is unbounded growth rather than any particular size -- a service with a legitimately large working set would sit permanently above a fixed threshold and train responders to ignore it. Both numbers need fitting to the deployment: the 5,000,000-entry projection should be set from the process memory limit divided by measured bytes per entry, and the 6h horizon should exceed the time needed to respond. Pair with a restart of the process as the immediate mitigation, since nothing else clears the cache while eviction is broken.

annotations.summary: kvstore has restarted more than once in the last hour
annotations.description: Detects the OOM chain after it has completed, and is deliberately independent of the cache instrumentation: it needs only the default process collectors, so it still fires if kvstore_cache_entries is wrong, missing, or itself the thing that broke. Repeated restarts with unbounded cache growth are the expected signature of OOM kills, since the cache refills from empty and grows to the same ceiling again. Treat a firing of this rule together with KvstoreCacheGrowthUnbounded as confirmation that memory, not a crash loop from some other cause, is the problem. Note the process also loses its entire cache on each restart, so stale-value and negative-entry symptoms will appear to resolve and then return.

annotations.summary: Writes are completing without invalidating the cached entry for the key
annotations.description: The earliest detection point in the stale-read chain: it fires at the moment staleness is created, rather than whenever a client eventually notices and complains. admin.update_value receives the Cache but never calls cache.evict(key), so any key already in the cache keeps serving its pre-write value -- and because Cache.get never re-consults storage for a cached key and eviction is broken, there is no fallback that ever reconciles the two. The fix is a single cache.evict(key) call after a successful put. This rule is self-retiring in the right way: once that lands the counter stays flat by construction, so the same series that exposed the bug proves the fix holds and catches its regression.

annotations.summary: Writes to the backing store are failing
annotations.description: Storage.put is raising StorageError -- a read-only filesystem, permissions, or a device error. Before the mr-write-outcomes instrumentation the write path emitted nothing at all on success or failure, so whether a write failure reached a human depended entirely on the external data-sync job's error handling, which lives outside this repository and is an assumption rather than a guarantee. This rule makes it observable from inside the service. Check the error_kind label to route: EACCES or EROFS is a deployment or configuration fault, ENOSPC is capacity and has its own rule. A failure landing mid-rewrite also destroys existing data, so check KvstoreStoreKeyCountDropped whenever this fires.

annotations.summary: The volume holding the kvstore backing file is out of space
annotations.description: Writes are failing with ENOSPC. This is more serious than an ordinary write failure because Storage.put truncates the only durable copy before writing the replacement: a rewrite that runs out of space part-way leaves the store shorter than it was, turning a capacity problem into permanent data loss. Treat as a data-loss incident, not merely a capacity one, and check KvstoreStoreKeyCountDropped immediately. Split from the general write-error rule on purpose -- the responder and the remediation differ, and the errno is available to make that distinction cheaply. Deliberately alerted from inside the service rather than from host filesystem metrics, which cannot confirm that this service's writes are the ones failing.

annotations.summary: No successful write has reached the backing store for over three hours
annotations.description: Detects writes stopping, whether because the periodic data-sync job was descheduled, crashed, or hung, or because every write it attempts is failing. Reads keep succeeding against increasingly old data throughout, so without this rule the only symptom is an absence that nothing in the service reports. Uses a timestamp gauge rather than a rate because rate() over a low or irregular write cadence cannot separate 'no writes attempted' from 'a genuinely quiet period', and stays meaningful across restarts and scrape gaps. THRESHOLD IS A PLACEHOLDER: 10800s assumes an hourly sync and allows three missed runs. The data-sync job's real period is not in the kvstore repository and must be supplied before this rule is enabled -- set the threshold to roughly three times the true period.

annotations.summary: The backing store has fewer keys than it did -- data has been lost
annotations.description: The store has no delete operation, so its key count is monotonically non-decreasing by construction and any drop is unambiguous evidence of loss rather than a threshold to tune. Causes are an interrupted whole-file rewrite (Storage.put truncates before writing, with no temp file and no atomic rename), a disk-full write, or two concurrent writers where the later one rewrites from a snapshot taken before the earlier one's change. Detection is necessarily after the fact -- the data is already gone when this fires -- so treat it as the trigger for restoring from backup, and note the real fix is a temp-file-and-rename write. One blind spot to be explicit about: a lost update to an existing key changes no count and is undetectable by any metric, findable only by comparing against the upstream source of truth.

annotations.summary: A write contained a key or value the flat-file format cannot represent
annotations.description: Storage writes pairs joined with a comma and parses them with partition(','), with no escaping on either side. A value containing a comma is silently truncated at the first one on read-back; a key or value containing a newline writes an extra physical line that is later parsed as a separate pair, letting one write fabricate or clobber an unrelated key. This fires at write time, the only point where the original uncorrupted value is still available -- afterwards the mangled value is a well-formed string indistinguishable from a correct one at every layer. Carries the critical severity of the corruption it causes rather than the warning severity of the format defect itself. Should be zero at all times, so no tuning is required.

annotations.summary: Reads are encountering unparseable lines in the backing store
annotations.description: A line with no delimiter or an empty key was found while scanning the store. Two causes, both worth waking someone for: a torn read, where a reader observed the file part-way through a non-atomic whole-file rewrite, or genuine on-disk corruption from an interrupted write. The torn-read case is transient and load-dependent, which makes it near-impossible to reconstruct from a user report after the fact -- catching it requires the observation to be made at the instant it happens, which is the whole reason this counter exists. Carries critical because it serves the corruption chain, though its other served mode is only a warning. Partial by nature: a tear landing on a clean line boundary produces no malformed line and stays invisible.

annotations.summary: p99 storage read latency is above 500ms
annotations.description: Every cache miss reads and linearly scans the entire backing file, so read latency is a direct function of total stored data rather than of the data requested. Clients see steadily worsening response times with no step change to point at. Measured at the storage layer rather than the API because API-level latency is diluted by the cache hit ratio, so the same underlying degradation appears there attenuated by an unknown and drifting factor. Warning rather than critical because it is degradation rather than outage -- but it is unbounded and ends in one, so treat a firing as a prompt to fix the O(file) read path rather than to raise the threshold. The 500ms value should be set from the latency clients can actually tolerate.

annotations.summary: The backing store file is projected to exceed 1GiB within a week
annotations.description: The store has no deletion operation and no compaction, so the file only ever grows. That matters on three axes at once: read cost, since every miss scans and materialises the whole file in memory; write cost, since every put rewrites it whole; and data-loss risk, since the non-atomic rewrite window widens with file size. Alerting on the projection rather than the current size gives time to act on what is otherwise a slow, silent trend nobody looks at. The 1GiB threshold and the one-week horizon are both starting points -- set the size from the memory the process can afford to spend materialising the file on every cache miss, which is the binding constraint here rather than disk.

payload_or_id.details: New metric: the current number of entries in Cache._entries, set on insert and on evict, or sampled by the eviction pass.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_cache_oldest_entry_age_seconds
payload_or_id.title: Age of the oldest live cache entry
payload_or_id.rationale: The most direct test of whether eviction works, and deliberately independent of why it does not: an entry older than TTL_SECONDS proves expiry is not happening, whether the cause is the seconds-vs-milliseconds arithmetic, a scheduler that never runs, or a future regression in either. payload_or_id.details: New metric: max(now - inserted_at) across live entries, computed during the eviction pass. Must be computed from the raw inserted_at value rather than by reusing the evictor's own comparison -- reusing the broken expression would produce a metric that agrees with the bug.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_eviction_passes_total
payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass execution counter
payload_or_id.rationale: Answers only 'did the pass run', one of the two independent questions eviction health needs. Kept separate from entries-removed on purpose: a scheduler that stopped firing and a pass that runs but evicts nothing are different faults with different fixes, and a single combined signal cannot tell an operator which one they have. Also remediates fm-eviction-progress-unobserved, excluded from alerting in its own right as an absence of instrumentation rather than a runtime condition.
payload_or_id.details: New metric, incremented at the end of every run_eviction_pass with outcome='success' or 'error'.

payload_or_id.title: Entries actually removed by eviction
payload_or_id.rationale: The cheapest possible detector of the live unit-mismatch bug: the pass always returns 0, so a counter that never advances is direct evidence. Not sufficient alone, because zero removals is legitimate when nothing has aged out yet; it becomes conclusive read together with mr-cache-oldest-entry-age, which establishes that something should have been removed.
payload_or_id.details: New metric: increment by run_eviction_pass's return value, which is computed today and then discarded by every caller.

payload_or_id.name: kvstore_cache_lookups_total
payload_or_id.title: Cache hit/miss counter, separating negative hits
payload_or_id.rationale: Separating negative hits from ordinary hits makes permanently-poisoned keys visible: a rising negative_hit rate means the service is confidently serving 'no such key' from memory without ever re-consulting storage. The hit ratio is also needed to interpret every other read-path signal -- with an unknown hit ratio, a flat storage-read rate is ambiguous between a healthy warm cache and a read path that has stopped reaching storage at all.
payload_or_id.details: New metric, emitted in Cache.get, with result in 'hit', 'negative_hit' (a cached Entry whose value is None), and 'miss'.

payload_or_id.rationale: Both operations touch the whole file, so their latency is a direct function of store size -- this turns a slow, unbounded degradation into something with a threshold. Also remediates fm-storage-linear-scan, excluded as a standing property.
payload_or_id.details: New metric wrapping Storage.get and Storage.put, labeled operation='get'|'put'.

A sudden decrease is the data-loss signal, and it is the only practical detector of truncation from an interrupted rewrite, a lost update, or a disk-full write: in a store with no delete operation the key count is monotonically non-decreasing by construction, so any drop is unambiguous evidence of loss rather than a threshold to tune.

annotations.summary: More than 1% of get_value calls are failing with StorageError
annotations.description: get_value is raising StorageError to clients, meaning cache misses are reaching the backing file and the read is failing -- permissions, a device error, a hung mount, or fd exhaustion. This is the only failure mode the pre-existing instrumentation could already detect, and the only one in kvstore that surfaces as an exception rather than as a wrong or absent value. The clamp_min guard keeps the ratio defined when traffic is zero, which would otherwise produce a 0/0 NaN and silently never fire. Serves the user-visible failure and its upstream cause with one rule deliberately: at this layer there is no remediation difference between them.

annotations.summary: get_value is failing with exceptions other than StorageError
annotations.description: Requests are failing in ways the original instrumentation could not see at all. Before the mr-api-catch-all-errors change, any exception other than StorageError incremented neither label, so such requests vanished from the total entirely and the error ratio was computed over a denominator that had silently dropped exactly the unanticipated failures an error-rate alert exists to catch. Any non-zero rate here is a bug worth a ticket. Note this rule cannot fire until that change lands -- it is recommended together with the instrumentation, not against today's code. A MemoryError appearing here is the last warning before the OOM chain completes and should be escalated immediately rather than triaged as a warning.

annotations.summary: The backing store file is missing -- reads are answering 'not found' for every key
annotations.description: Storage.get is taking its file-does-not-exist branch, which returns None rather than raising. Every read is therefore answering 'key not found' and, without the mr-storage-read-results split, would be counted as outcome='success' -- a complete data outage reported as perfect health. Likely causes are a deleted file, an unmounted or empty-mounted volume, or a wrong path in configuration. The cache compounds it: each such read is stored as a permanent negative entry, so the fault survives the file being restored and may require a process restart to clear. This series should be zero at all times, so the threshold needs no baseline and no tuning; the 2m for_duration exists only to ride out a scrape landing mid-deploy.

annotations.summary: Over half of get_value calls are returning no value
annotations.description: The client-visible end of the data-outage chain: the service is answering 'no such key' for the majority of requests. Complements KvstoreStorageFileAbsent rather than duplicating it -- the storage-layer signal fades as the cache fills with permanent negative entries, and this one takes over at exactly that point, because it is measured where clients actually experience the failure. It also catches the poisoned-key case, where a read that arrived before the data-sync job wrote the key leaves a negative entry that never expires. The 0.5 threshold is the one number here that depends on the workload: a service whose clients legitimately probe for absent keys needs it raised, and the correct value should be read off the not_found ratio during known-good operation before this rule is enabled.

annotations.summary: A large share of reads are served 'no such key' from cache without consulting storage
annotations.description: Cache.get is returning cached None values, meaning the service is confidently answering 'no such key' from memory for keys it has not re-checked against storage since the first miss. Because negative entries are cached with the same permanence as real values and eviction is the only thing that would ever clear them, a rising ratio means an accumulating population of keys that can never become visible even after they are written. Scoped to this single failure mode on purpose, and kept at warning: the user-visible consequences are alerted separately by KvstoreNotFoundRatioHigh at critical, and promoting this rule to match would page on a ratio that is legitimately high for workloads that probe for absent keys. The 30m for_duration reflects that this is an accumulating condition, not a step change.

annotations.summary: Cache entries are surviving well past their TTL -- expiry is not working
annotations.description: An entry is alive at more than twice TTL_SECONDS (300s), which proves expiry is not happening. Deliberately indifferent to why: it fires for the known seconds-versus-milliseconds bug in run_eviction_pass, for a scheduler that never invokes the pass, and for any future regression in either, so it keeps working after the current bug is fixed. This is also the closest available bound on staleness exposure -- entry age bounds how old a served value can be -- which is why it serves the stale-read and invisible-key chains as well. The 600s threshold is 2x TTL and must be raised together with TTL_SECONDS if that constant ever changes; the two are coupled and will drift apart silently otherwise.

annotations.summary: The eviction pass is running but removing nothing while entries are past TTL
annotations.description: The sharper diagnosis of the same fault KvstoreCacheEntriesNeverExpire detects, kept separate because it points an operator at the code rather than at the scheduler. Neither half is conclusive alone: zero removals is entirely legitimate when nothing has aged out yet, and an old entry could be explained by a pass that has not run recently. Together they are conclusive -- something should have been removed and was not. This is the exact signature of the live bug, where run_eviction_pass compares a seconds-based now against a milliseconds-based inserted_at, making the expired condition permanently false and the return value permanently 0.

annotations.summary: Nothing has invoked the eviction pass recently
annotations.description: Answers the separate question 'did the pass run at all', which is what tells an operator to look at the scheduler rather than at the eviction code. run_eviction_pass has no caller anywhere in the kvstore repository, so the scheduler is external and may never have been wired up, may be misconfigured to too long an interval, or may have died. This is independent of the arithmetic bug: fixing that leaves eviction just as dead if nothing calls the function, and eviction is the only thing bounding cache memory. The absent() arm matters as much as the increase() arm, because a pass that has never run once produces no series to compare against.

annotations.summary: Cache is on track to exhaust memory within hours
annotations.description: The leading indicator for the OOM chain, and the only rule in this set that gives time to act before a total outage: the pre-existing request counter looks perfectly healthy right up to the moment the process is killed, then simply stops. Uses predict_linear rather than a static ceiling because the failure is unbounded growth rather than any particular size -- a service with a legitimately large working set would sit permanently above a fixed threshold and train responders to ignore it. Both numbers need fitting to the deployment: the 5,000,000-entry projection should be set from the process memory limit divided by measured bytes per entry, and the 6h horizon should exceed the time needed to respond. Pair with a restart of the process as the immediate mitigation, since nothing else clears the cache while eviction is broken.

annotations.summary: kvstore has restarted more than once in the last hour
annotations.description: Detects the OOM chain after it has completed, and is deliberately independent of the cache instrumentation: it needs only the default process collectors, so it still fires if kvstore_cache_entries is wrong, missing, or itself the thing that broke. Repeated restarts with unbounded cache growth are the expected signature of OOM kills, since the cache refills from empty and grows to the same ceiling again. Treat a firing of this rule together with KvstoreCacheGrowthUnbounded as confirmation that memory, not a crash loop from some other cause, is the problem. Note the process also loses its entire cache on each restart, so stale-value and negative-entry symptoms will appear to resolve and then return.

annotations.summary: Writes are completing without invalidating the cached entry for the key
annotations.description: The earliest detection point in the stale-read chain: it fires at the moment staleness is created, rather than whenever a client eventually notices and complains. admin.update_value receives the Cache but never calls cache.evict(key), so any key already in the cache keeps serving its pre-write value -- and because Cache.get never re-consults storage for a cached key and eviction is broken, there is no fallback that ever reconciles the two. The fix is a single cache.evict(key) call after a successful put. This rule is self-retiring in the right way: once that lands the counter stays flat by construction, so the same series that exposed the bug proves the fix holds and catches its regression.

annotations.summary: Writes to the backing store are failing
annotations.description: Storage.put is raising StorageError -- a read-only filesystem, permissions, or a device error. Before the mr-write-outcomes instrumentation the write path emitted nothing at all on success or failure, so whether a write failure reached a human depended entirely on the external data-sync job's error handling, which lives outside this repository and is an assumption rather than a guarantee. This rule makes it observable from inside the service. Check the error_kind label to route: EACCES or EROFS is a deployment or configuration fault, ENOSPC is capacity and has its own rule. A failure landing mid-rewrite also destroys existing data, so check KvstoreStoreKeyCountDropped whenever this fires.

annotations.summary: The volume holding the kvstore backing file is out of space
annotations.description: Writes are failing with ENOSPC. This is more serious than an ordinary write failure because Storage.put truncates the only durable copy before writing the replacement: a rewrite that runs out of space part-way leaves the store shorter than it was, turning a capacity problem into permanent data loss. Treat as a data-loss incident, not merely a capacity one, and check KvstoreStoreKeyCountDropped immediately. Split from the general write-error rule on purpose -- the responder and the remediation differ, and the errno is available to make that distinction cheaply. Deliberately alerted from inside the service rather than from host filesystem metrics, which cannot confirm that this service's writes are the ones failing.

annotations.summary: No successful write has reached the backing store for over three hours
annotations.description: Detects writes stopping, whether because the periodic data-sync job was descheduled, crashed, or hung, or because every write it attempts is failing. Reads keep succeeding against increasingly old data throughout, so without this rule the only symptom is an absence that nothing in the service reports. Uses a timestamp gauge rather than a rate because rate() over a low or irregular write cadence cannot separate 'no writes attempted' from 'a genuinely quiet period', and stays meaningful across restarts and scrape gaps. THRESHOLD IS A PLACEHOLDER: 10800s assumes an hourly sync and allows three missed runs. The data-sync job's real period is not in the kvstore repository and must be supplied before this rule is enabled -- set the threshold to roughly three times the true period.

annotations.summary: The backing store has fewer keys than it did -- data has been lost
annotations.description: The store has no delete operation, so its key count is monotonically non-decreasing by construction and any drop is unambiguous evidence of loss rather than a threshold to tune. Causes are an interrupted whole-file rewrite (Storage.put truncates before writing, with no temp file and no atomic rename), a disk-full write, or two concurrent writers where the later one rewrites from a snapshot taken before the earlier one's change. Detection is necessarily after the fact -- the data is already gone when this fires -- so treat it as the trigger for restoring from backup, and note the real fix is a temp-file-and-rename write. One blind spot to be explicit about: a lost update to an existing key changes no count and is undetectable by any metric, findable only by comparing against the upstream source of truth.

annotations.summary: A write contained a key or value the flat-file format cannot represent
annotations.description: Storage writes pairs joined with a comma and parses them with partition(','), with no escaping on either side. A value containing a comma is silently truncated at the first one on read-back; a key or value containing a newline writes an extra physical line that is later parsed as a separate pair, letting one write fabricate or clobber an unrelated key. This fires at write time, the only point where the original uncorrupted value is still available -- afterwards the mangled value is a well-formed string indistinguishable from a correct one at every layer. Carries the critical severity of the corruption it causes rather than the warning severity of the format defect itself. Should be zero at all times, so no tuning is required.

annotations.summary: Reads are encountering unparseable lines in the backing store
annotations.description: A line with no delimiter or an empty key was found while scanning the store. Two causes, both worth waking someone for: a torn read, where a reader observed the file part-way through a non-atomic whole-file rewrite, or genuine on-disk corruption from an interrupted write. The torn-read case is transient and load-dependent, which makes it near-impossible to reconstruct from a user report after the fact -- catching it requires the observation to be made at the instant it happens, which is the whole reason this counter exists. Carries critical because it serves the corruption chain, though its other served mode is only a warning. Partial by nature: a tear landing on a clean line boundary produces no malformed line and stays invisible.

annotations.summary: p99 storage read latency is above 500ms
annotations.description: Every cache miss reads and linearly scans the entire backing file, so read latency is a direct function of total stored data rather than of the data requested. Clients see steadily worsening response times with no step change to point at. Measured at the storage layer rather than the API because API-level latency is diluted by the cache hit ratio, so the same underlying degradation appears there attenuated by an unknown and drifting factor. Warning rather than critical because it is degradation rather than outage -- but it is unbounded and ends in one, so treat a firing as a prompt to fix the O(file) read path rather than to raise the threshold. The 500ms value should be set from the latency clients can actually tolerate.

annotations.summary: The backing store file is projected to exceed 1GiB within a week
annotations.description: The store has no deletion operation and no compaction, so the file only ever grows. That matters on three axes at once: read cost, since every miss scans and materialises the whole file in memory; write cost, since every put rewrites it whole; and data-loss risk, since the non-atomic rewrite window widens with file size. Alerting on the projection rather than the current size gives time to act on what is otherwise a slow, silent trend nobody looks at. The 1GiB threshold and the one-week horizon are both starting points -- set the size from the memory the process can afford to spend materialising the file on every cache miss, which is the binding constraint here rather than disk.

annotations.summary: kvstore is not being scraped -- every other kvstore alert is currently blind
annotations.description: The kvstore scrape target is down or has never existed. This alert is a precondition for every other rule in this set: no exposition endpoint is started anywhere in the kvstore repository, so if none is wired up outside it, all kvstore metrics are written to a registry nobody reads and every other alert here is silently unfirable while appearing to be full coverage. The absent() arm is the important half -- a target that was never configured produces no series at all, so a rule testing only up == 0 would itself be silent. Check that the process starts a prometheus_client exposition endpoint and that the scrape config targets it.

payload_or_id.rationale: The implemented counter already suffices. A StorageError propagating out of get_value increments outcome='error' at kvstore/api.py:30, so the rate of that series against the total is a working detector and only an alert rule is missing.

Already detectable with the implemented counter: an unreadable file is wrapped as StorageError and surfaces as outcome='error'. The same series covers this upstream cause and its user-visible end, fm-read-unavailable, so one alert rule serves both -- which is correct here, because at this layer there is no remediation difference between them. mr-storage-read-results would additionally separate a read error from other storage outcomes, but that is a diagnostic improvement rather than a detection gap, so this stays alertable.

Undetectable today: every stale read is counted as outcome='success', and no signal distinguishes a fresh value from an arbitrarily old one. mr-write-leaves-stale-cache catches it at the earliest possible link, the moment a write leaves a live cache entry in place, rather than when a client eventually complains; mr-cache-oldest-entry-age bounds how stale a served value can be and catches the case where invalidation is fixed but expiry is still broken.

Undetectable today: a permanently-poisoned negative cache entry returns None and is counted as a success. mr-cache-lookups makes negative hits visible as a distinct series, which is the specific signature of this mode; mr-api-outcome-not-found makes the client-visible symptom countable; mr-cache-oldest-entry-age shows that the poisoned entry is never aging out.

The existing counter gives no warning at all -- it looks healthy until the process dies, at which point the series simply stops. mr-cache-entries is the leading indicator that makes growth visible with time to act; mr-metrics-exposition adds resident memory and process start time as an independent confirmation that does not depend on the cache gauge being correct; mr-api-catch-all-errors recovers the MemoryError that is currently swallowed uncounted on the way down.

The highest-consequence blind spot in the service: a deleted file or unmounted volume yields a 100% success rate. mr-storage-read-results gives an unambiguous, should-always-be-zero signal at the point of the fault; mr-api-outcome-not-found gives the client-visible ratio; mr-cache-lookups explains why the storage-layer signal fades over time as the cache fills with negative entries, which is exactly when the API-layer one takes over.

No signal whatsoever today -- a mangled value is a well-formed string returned as a success, so corruption is indistinguishable from correctness at every layer. Both recommendations are should-always-be-zero counters placed at the moment the corruption is created or observed, since there is no way to detect it after the fact from the value alone.

Currently invisible: lost keys read back as 'not found' with a success outcome. mr-storage-size is the detector that matters, because the store has no delete operation and so its key count is monotonically non-decreasing by construction -- any drop is unambiguous evidence of loss and needs no threshold. mr-write-outcomes catches the interrupted or failed write that caused it, and mr-storage-read-results catches the total-loss case.

No latency is measured anywhere in the service today, at any layer. mr-storage-op-duration measures it where the cost actually lives, undiluted by the cache hit ratio; mr-storage-size gives the underlying driver, so an operator sees the cause and the symptom together and can act before the threshold is crossed.

Requires alerting on absence, which nothing in the service currently supports: no signal distinguishes 'writes stopped' from 'nothing to write'. mr-last-write-timestamp turns that into a direct staleness expression comparable against the job's known period; mr-write-outcomes separates the two causes -- a job that stopped running from one that is running and failing every write.

The live bug, and entirely invisible: the pass returns 0 and completes normally, which reads as working. mr-eviction-entries-removed plus mr-cache-oldest-entry-age together are conclusive -- zero removals is legitimate on its own, but zero removals while an entry is older than TTL_SECONDS is not. mr-cache-oldest-entry-age is deliberately computed from raw inserted_at rather than the evictor's own comparison, so the metric cannot inherit the bug it exists to detect.

Invisible today, and indistinguishable from the unit-mismatch bug because both produce identical evidence: none. mr-eviction-passes answers the separate question 'did the pass run at all', which is what tells an operator whether to look at the scheduler or at the code. mr-cache-entries confirms the consequence.

No signal today -- the missing cache.evict call is a silent omission with no runtime trace. mr-write-leaves-stale-cache detects it directly at the write, and is self-retiring in the right way: once the evict call is added the counter stays flat by construction, so the same series that exposes the bug also proves the fix and catches its regression.

Not observable today, and it is the multiplier that turns two transient faults into permanent per-key ones. mr-cache-lookups separates negative_hit from hit, which is the only way to see the service confidently serving 'no such key' from memory without re-consulting storage.

Nothing measures the store's size today. mr-storage-size makes the trend visible far enough ahead to act, which matters because growth also raises the cost of every write and widens the non-atomic rewrite window; mr-storage-op-duration shows when that growth starts costing users.

The truncation window itself cannot be observed directly, so detection has to be of its consequence: mr-storage-size shows the key count dropping after an interrupted rewrite. Worth stating plainly that this is after-the-fact detection -- the data is already gone by the time it fires, and the real fix is a temp-file-and-rename write. The metric earns its place by making loss discoverable in minutes rather than whenever someone asks for a missing key.

Detectable only in the case where the lost update was a new key, which mr-storage-size catches as a key count that fails to advance or drops. A lost update to an existing key changes no count and remains undetectable by any metric -- it is only findable by comparing against the source of truth, which is outside this service. Recorded as a partial-coverage gap rather than a solved one, and its reachability depends on whether the data-sync job is ever concurrent with itself, which the repository does not settle.

Transient and load-dependent, so it is near-impossible to reconstruct from a user report after the fact -- the observation has to be made at the instant it happens. mr-storage-malformed-lines catches the parse anomaly a truncated file produces. Partial by nature: a torn read that happens to end on a clean line boundary yields no malformed line and stays invisible.

Silent today in both directions -- neither the write that creates unrepresentable data nor the read that mangles it leaves any trace. mr-storage-unencodable-pairs catches it at write time, which is the only point where the original, uncorrupted value is still available to compare against.

The service emits nothing on the write path, so today this reaches a human only if the external data-sync job happens to handle and report it -- an assumption about code outside this repository. mr-write-outcomes makes it observable from inside the service, and its error_kind label separates the responders: EACCES or EROFS is a deployment fault, not a capacity one.

The single highest-value gap to close: the branch that conflates 'I have no data' with 'the key is not there' is what makes total data loss silent. mr-storage-read-results gives result='file_absent' its own series, which should be zero at all times, so the alert needs no baseline and cannot be masked by normal not-found traffic.

No service-level signal today. mr-write-outcomes with error_kind='ENOSPC' detects it at the point of failure; mr-storage-size gives the growth trend leading up to it. Deliberately not marked alertable on the assumption that host filesystem metrics exist: node-level disk monitoring is outside this repository and cannot be verified from here, and free space on the host would in any case not tell an operator that this service's writes are the ones failing.

Cannot be detected by any existing signal, because the symptom is an absence and the service has no notion of expected write cadence. mr-last-write-timestamp supplies exactly that, as a value that keeps growing when the job stops. Its threshold is the one recommendation here that needs a fact from outside the repository -- the job's actual period -- which is called out for phase 4.

Total blind spot: the write path emits nothing on success or failure, so a job that runs on schedule and fails every write looks identical to one succeeding. mr-write-outcomes closes it directly, and is a prerequisite for trusting any conclusion drawn about write-path health, including the staleness chain above.

Cannot be detected by the service's own metrics, since that is circular -- it has to be detected by the scrape layer, as an absent target or up == 0. mr-metrics-exposition is a prerequisite for every other row in this table rather than a peer of them: if no sink is wired up outside this repository, every alert recommended in phase 4 is dead while appearing to be full coverage. Verification is called out as a precondition rather than assumed.

A defect in the one implemented metric, so it degrades every conclusion drawn from it: unanticipated failures increment neither label and vanish from the denominator, which is precisely the class of failure an error-rate alert exists to catch. mr-api-catch-all-errors is a change to the existing counter rather than a new metric, and it should land before any error-ratio alert is trusted.
